regarding synthesizing: will add support for synthesizing root. But nobody is problematic: the definition of nobody might differ between host and root environment, hence we probably shouldn't apply the host's compiled-in defaults to the image.
Force pushed new version. Split out the offline stuff into own .c file with own functions. Also synthesizing root now. ptal!

> regarding synthesizing: will add support for synthesizing root.

Great, thanks.

> But nobody is problematic: the definition of nobody might differ between host and root environment, hence we probably shouldn't apply the host's compiled-in defaults to the image.

I'd argue that this is applying the defaults compiled into *systemd-tmpfiles*, which we are already implicitly doing since systemd-tmpfiles changes behaviour a bit in different versions. But yeah, `root` is the important one, and nobody is probably very rarely used.

Most cross-compilation systems already have a specific host-systemd recompiled anyway... split-user means we can't trust the host's systemd and we have to compile our own to run systemctl preset-all.

So trusting the compiled-in name and value for nobody makes sense since it's a custom-built host-systemd with the correct values for the target system.

Yes, you can always override the default by adding root/nobody to the target rootfs config files (and potentially removing those again after running systemd-tmpfiles). This is not really an arguments for/against synthesized users, but if you bootstrap a target system you will either use a fitting tool or fitting config files for the setup.

Now for something completely different, sysusers already does a similar thing (reading passwd/group database). It would make sense to unify and separate the code involved.

so yeah, i started out sharing this, but then i removed it again because the double indexing sysusers needs was too complex for tmpfiles, and it didn't appear worth it... dunno. maybe merge as is? prep a PR that unifies this afterwards, if its good and clean?

issue_context.title: Support uid/gids from target rootfs when using the --root option
issue_context.body:
*Problem*

I would like to prepare an rootfs for embedded, as read-only as possible.
This would include creating all files/directory on a different system, typically this is done in an **fakeroot** environment to allow creating archives with correct permissings and uids/gids.

To this effect, `tmpfilesd` sould be run in a similar fashion to this:
```bash
systemd-tmpfiles --root=ROOTFS --create --boot --exclude-prefix=/dev --exclude-prefix=/tmp
```

The issue is that `systemd-tmpfiles` uses the uid/gids from the hosting PC, not the ones from the target filesystem. For example `/var/log/journal` will almost certainly not end up with the correct gid in the target filesystem.

I attached a testcase that should demonstrate the issue

**The solution I would like**

`systemd-tmpfiles` (and potentially others creating files with uid/gid other than 0) should parse the 'ROOTFS/etc/{passwd,group}' files when the '--root' argument was provided, then use this database only for file modification (and checks)

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Unfortunately there is no `fakeroot` alternative that could transparently modify the library calls,
`fakeroot` cant resolve names differently to the running filesystem.

Some `chroot` trickery would be possibly, but that needs root access, and might be really tricky if the target architecure is different.

[testcase.tar.gz](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/4164869/testcase.tar.gz)
comments:
Does systemd-sysuser have the same problem ?

Right now buildroot creates all users at build time using a script of its own but one of my plan was to move that to calling sysuser with --root at build time....

Seems like sysusers does load the databases manually, was almost certain it doesnt. SO I guess it wont have the problem.

Btw. I just posted a set of patches to BR mailing list, might tale a look there so we don't step on each others toes
There are no nice apis to do NSS relative to some root dir, that's the problem here.

If I use the `--root` argument, chances are I don't need a running NSS. (I'm serious, what are the use cases other than preparing a dormant, separate filesystem for this argument? ).

The "filesystem" database should suffice, code for that is already in sysuser tool. Resolve names via passwd/group file and set the raw uid/gids.

review_comments: I'd feel more comfortable if this reading was split out to a function. It'd be good to even put all of this new code (the parts to read and query `passwd` and `group` offline) in a separate file so we can add a test for this in the future.
